evals.name: draft-a-pr-faq-from-scratch
evals.prompt: I'm a PM at a Series C fintech (~250 people, $30M ARR). We're considering building an in-app expense-approval workflow for our SMB customers. Right now they export a CSV, upload to their accounting tool, and someone manually approves each line. Our engineering team is excited because we already have the transaction data and could ship an MVP in 6 weeks. Help me think about whether we should build this using Bill Carr and Colin Bryar's Working Backwards method — help me draft the PR/FAQ.
evals.expected_output: Output should: (a) push back on the skills-forward framing (starting from 'we already have the data' is exactly the failure mode the PR/FAQ is designed to prevent); (b) force the customer question to be answered specifically before drafting anything (who exactly, what atomic need, why now, how would we know we solved it); (c) walk through the Press Release structure (heading, subheading, summary, problem, solution, quotes, getting started); (d) prompt for both External and Internal FAQ sections; (e) name the risk that most PR/FAQs get rejected and that's the point; (f) cite Carr, Bryar, or the book at least once; (g) NOT jump straight to writing the doc without first testing the customer-need articulation.
assertions: Output challenges the skills-forward framing ('engineering is excited because we already have the data') using attribution
Output forces the customer question to be answered specifically before drafting the press release
Output names all Press Release sections (heading, subheading, summary, problem, solution, quotes, getting started)
Output distinguishes External FAQ from Internal FAQ and names what belongs in each
Output explicitly notes that most PR/FAQs are and should be rejected
Output cites Bill Carr, Colin Bryar, the book, workingbackwards.com, or a specific podcast/blog source at least once
Output does NOT jump straight to drafting the press release without validating the customer-need articulation
Output uses the term 'PR/FAQ' (uppercase, with slash) — not 'PRFAQ' or 'PR faq'

evals.name: critique-a-doc-that-is-really-a-feature-announcement
evals.prompt:
Please critique this PR/FAQ I wrote against the Working Backwards method.

---

PRESS RELEASE: Introducing SmartApprove, the World's Most Advanced Expense Approval Engine

Today we're excited to announce SmartApprove, a revolutionary AI-powered expense approval workflow that will transform how businesses handle their finances. Built on our industry-leading transaction data platform, SmartApprove leverages cutting-edge machine learning to deliver unparalleled efficiency gains.

SmartApprove seamlessly integrates with our existing platform to deliver a world-class expense management experience. Customers will love the intuitive interface, powerful automation, and best-in-class security.

"SmartApprove is a game-changer," said our CEO. "It's the future of expense management."

FAQ:

Q: When is it available?
A: Q3 2026.

Q: How much does it cost?
A: Included in Premium tier.

Q: What's the technology stack?
A: Python, React, PostgreSQL, GPT-4.

---

Review this against Working Backwards.
evals.expected_output: Output should identify that this is NOT a PR/FAQ — it's a marketing announcement with a hyperbole-riddled press release, a wishy-washy FAQ, and no actual customer-need articulation. Specifically it should: (a) name the hyperbole ('revolutionary', 'world's most advanced', 'game-changer', 'world-class', 'best-in-class') and cite Carr's rule about factual writing without hyperbole; (b) note there is no problem paragraph — the customer's specific problem is not named; (c) note the customer is not named specifically at all; (d) note the solution starts from company capabilities ('built on our platform') not customer need; (e) note there is no Internal FAQ (finance, ops, technical strategic concerns are missing); (f) note the External FAQ is thin — no comparison to alternatives, no adoption question, no TAM; (g) probably cite Carr's Lenny 2023 quote about being factual and data-rich, not hyperbolic.
assertions: Output identifies this as a marketing announcement / feature pitch rather than a real PR/FAQ
Output names the hyperbole problem with at least 2 specific examples ('revolutionary', 'world-class', 'game-changer', 'best-in-class', 'unparalleled')
Output cites Bill Carr's rule about factual, non-hyperbolic writing (with attribution)
Output identifies that the customer is not named specifically
Output identifies that the problem paragraph is missing or vague
Output identifies that the solution is skills-forward (starts from company capabilities, not customer need)
Output identifies that the Internal FAQ is missing or that the FAQs don't do the interrogation job
Output cites at least one specific source (book, blog post, or podcast episode)

evals.name: voice-check-user-wants-shortcut
evals.prompt: We're a fast-moving team and we don't have three months to write a PR/FAQ before shipping. Can you just help me put together an Amazon-style memo template we can drop into our team? We already do customer research so the customer-first thing is covered.
evals.expected_output: Output should push back on the shortcut framing in a Carr-consistent way — measured, not preachy, but firm. Specifically it should: (a) name that 'template alone' isn't the mechanism (the review discipline is); (b) reference Carr's 'slow is smooth and smooth is fast' tagline; (c) name that customer research feeding into a document is not the same as the PR/FAQ review discipline; (d) redirect the user toward either committing to the mechanism honestly (with CEO air cover) or considering a lighter shape more appropriate for their team's stage (Continuous Discovery / Lean Startup); (e) NOT sell adoption as easy or offer a 'lite' version that dilutes the mechanism.
assertions: Output pushes back on the 'just give me the template' framing rather than complying with it
Output cites Bill Carr's 'slow is smooth and smooth is fast' or an equivalent shortcut-resistant quote
Output distinguishes the template from the mechanism (review discipline, silent reading, most PR/FAQs rejected)
Output either redirects to a lighter framework (Lean Startup, Continuous Discovery) OR names what full-mechanism commitment would require
Output does NOT sell adoption as easy or promise a frictionless transformation
Response tone is measured and operator-like (not preachy or contrarian)

evals.name: diagnose-fractional-stl
evals.prompt: We just named a Single-Threaded Leader for our new AI-powered onboarding initiative. Sarah is going to lead it — she's a fantastic senior PM. She'll continue leading her current two product areas (about 60% of her time) and take on the AI onboarding initiative (about 40%). We've assigned two engineers and a designer to help, though they're also supporting other teams. I think we're set up well — thoughts?
evals.expected_output: Output should identify that this is NOT a Single-Threaded Leader — it's a fractionally-threaded lead with a fancy title. Specifically it should: (a) name that STL requires zero competing responsibilities; (b) name that STL requires dedicated (not matrixed) cross-functional resources; (c) reference Bill Carr's quote about creating teams that can stand alone with dedicated cross-functional resources; (d) name that this is the pre-STL state Amazon rejected around 2004-2005; (e) offer the choice honestly — either dedicate Sarah fully (and dedicate the eng/design resources), or don't call it an STL; (f) probably reference the coordination-tax framing from the March 2026 firm blog.
assertions: Output identifies that this is NOT a real STL
Output names at least 2 of the mandatory STL conditions being violated (one leader / zero competing / dedicated resources / separable structure)
Output cites Bill Carr, the book, or a specific firm source when explaining the STL mechanism
Output offers a specific concrete choice (dedicate Sarah fully OR don't call it STL)
Output does NOT congratulate the user or accept the fractional-STL as 'set up well'
Output uses the STL terminology correctly (STL / STO distinction if relevant)
